what: ⚠️ CRITICAL: Worktree Requirement for Parallel Agents
title: CLAUDE.md
text: Multiple agents MUST use separate git worktrees. Working directory causes file conflicts. matters: Without worktrees, parallel agents modify files, causing: - Uncommitted changes one agent appearing another’s work - Merge conflicts within working directory - Lost mixed work features
code: # BEFORE starting work, check if you're in a worktree or the main repo git rev-parse --show-toplevel  # If another agent might be working, create your own worktree: git worktree add ../measure.sec-<issue-id> -b feat/<short-description> cd ../measure.sec-<issue-id>

title: Polymer Branching Analysis

title: Polymer Branching Analysis
text: sample linear reference molecular weight, measure_branching_index() calculates g=Rg2(sample)Rg2(linear reference).g = \frac{R_g^2(\text{sample})}{R_g^2(\text{linear reference})}. value 1 means sample smaller radius gyration reference molecular weight. interpretation depends quality range reference data; example uses three supplied linear reference values. Rg-based branching index calculated synthetic sample-level properties supplied linear reference. dashed line marks g = 1, linear-reference value.
code: linear_ref <- sample_properties |>   filter(topology == "linear") |>   select(mw, rg) |>   arrange(mw)  branch100 <- sample_properties |>   filter(sample_id == "Branch-100K")  g_result <- measure_branching_index(   mw = branch100$mw,   rg = branch100$rg,   reference = linear_ref,   method = "g" )  print(g_result) #> Branching Analysis Results #> ==================================================  #>  #> MW Range: 100000 - 100000 #> g (Rg ratio): 0.627 - 0.627 (mean: 0.627) #>  #> Estimated branches/molecule: 2.6 - 2.6 #>  #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>       mw     g #>    <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 100000 0.627  branching_results <- sample_properties |>   mutate(     g = vapply(       seq_len(nrow(sample_properties)),       function(i) {         measure_branching_index(           mw = sample_properties$mw[i],           rg = sample_properties$rg[i],           reference = linear_ref,           method = "g"         )$g[[1]]       },       numeric(1)     )   )  branching_results #> # A tibble: 8 × 7 #>   sample_id   topology     mw branching_index    rg intrinsic_visc     g #>   <chr>       <chr>     <dbl>           <dbl> <dbl>          <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 Branch-50K  branched  50000            0.75   7               34 0.678 #> 2 Linear-50K  linear    50000            1      8.5             45 1     #> 3 Star-50K    star      50000            0.6    5.8             27 0.466 #> 4 Branch-100K branched 100000            0.65   9.5             47 0.627 #> 5 Linear-100K linear   100000            1     12               72 1     #> 6 Star-100K   star     100000            0.5    7.5             36 0.391 #> 7 Branch-200K branched 200000            0.55  12.5             63 0.541 #> 8 Linear-200K linear   200000            1     17              115 1 ggplot(   branching_results,   aes(x = mw, y = g, colour = topology, shape = topology) ) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +   geom_line(aes(group = topology), linewidth = 0.6) +   geom_point(size = 2.4) +   scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +   scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)) +   scale_colour_manual(     values = c(linear = "#2E86AB", branched = "#A23B72", star = "#3B7A57")   ) +   labs(     x = "Molecular weight (Da)",     y = "Rg-based branching index, g",     colour = "Topology",     shape = "Topology"   ) +   theme_measure_sec()

title: Polymer Branching Analysis
text: measure_branching_frequency() maps g branches per molecule specified architecture. , g value Branch-100K passed four models. results model-dependent estimates, direct counts branch points. Branch-count estimates Branch-100K g value four architecture assumptions. bar result returned measure_branching_frequency() model.
code: g_for_frequency <- g_result$g[[1]] architectures <- c("random", "star_3", "star_4", "comb")  frequency_results <- tibble::tibble(   architecture = architectures,   branches_per_molecule = vapply(     architectures,     function(architecture) {       measure_branching_frequency(         g = g_for_frequency,         architecture = architecture       )$branches_per_molecule[[1]]     },     numeric(1)   ) )  frequency_results #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #>   architecture branches_per_molecule #>   <chr>                        <dbl> #> 1 random                       7.74  #> 2 star_3                       1     #> 3 star_4                       1     #> 4 comb                         0.893 ggplot(   frequency_results,   aes(x = architecture, y = branches_per_molecule) ) +   geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "#2E86AB") +   labs(     x = "Assumed architecture",     y = "Estimated branches per molecule"   ) +   theme_measure_sec()

title: Polymer Branching Analysis
text: Mark-Houwink equation relates intrinsic viscosity molecular weight: [η]=KMa.[\eta] = K M^. exponent depends polymer, solvent, temperature, molecular-weight range. points use sample-level values synthetic dataset; lines descriptive log-log fits linear branched samples. Sample-level intrinsic viscosity values log-log linear fits supplied linear branched examples. point one distinct sample, one elution-time row.
code: linear_data <- sample_properties |>   filter(topology == "linear", intrinsic_visc > 0)  mh <- measure_mh_parameters(   mw = linear_data$mw,   intrinsic_visc = linear_data$intrinsic_visc )  print(mh) #> Mark-Houwink Parameters #> ========================================  #>  #> K = 2.9716e-02 #> a = 0.677 #>  #> R-squared: 1.0000 #> Data points: 3 #> MW range: 50000 - 200000 #>  #> Equation: [eta] = K * M^a  mh_comparison <- sample_properties |>   filter(topology %in% c("linear", "branched")) ggplot(   mh_comparison,   aes(x = mw, y = intrinsic_visc, colour = topology, shape = topology) ) +   geom_point(size = 2.5) +   geom_smooth(     method = "lm",     formula = y ~ x,     se = FALSE,     linewidth = 0.7   ) +   scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +   scale_y_log10() +   scale_colour_manual(     values = c(linear = "#2E86AB", branched = "#A23B72")   ) +   labs(     x = "Molecular weight (Da)",     y = "Intrinsic viscosity (mL/g)",     colour = "Topology",     shape = "Topology"   ) +   theme_measure_sec()

code: # Load polystyrene standards data(sec_ps_standards)  # View the standards sec_ps_standards |>   select(standard_name, mp, log_mp, retention_time) |>   head(8) #> # A tibble: 8 × 4 #>   standard_name      mp log_mp retention_time #>   <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl>          <dbl> #> 1 PS-3150000    3150000   6.50           11.2 #> 2 PS-1870000    1870000   6.27           11.6 #> 3 PS-1090000    1090000   6.04           12.1 #> 4 PS-630000      630000   5.80           12.6 #> 5 PS-430000      430000   5.63           13.2 #> 6 PS-216000      216000   5.33           13.8 #> 7 PS-120000      120000   5.08           14.3 #> 8 PS-67500        67500   4.83           15.0 # Prepare standards with required column names # The step expects 'retention' and 'log_mw' columns ps_cal_standards <- sec_ps_standards |>   select(retention = retention_time, log_mw = log_mp)  data(sec_triple_detect, package = "measure.sec") sample_data <- sec_triple_detect |>   filter(sample_id == "PS-50K")  # Create a recipe with conventional calibration rec <- recipe(ri_signal + elution_time ~ sample_id, data = sample_data) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   ) |>   step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri") |>   step_sec_conventional_cal(     measures = "ri",     standards = ps_cal_standards,     fit_type = "cubic",     extrapolation = "none"   )  # Prep the recipe (this fits the calibration) prepped <- prep(rec) #> Warning: Standard at 12.58 has 14.4% MW deviation. #> ℹ Consider removing outlier standards or using a different fit type.

what: Check signed RI conversion before normalization
title: Qualify SEC detector units, delays and clipped signal
text: instrument_constant positive conversion gain: multiplying recorded signal gives calibrated refractive-index difference. Dividing difference dn_dc mL/g gives concentration g/mL. negative increment can therefore turn negative RI response positive concentration without taking absolute value detector trace. Brookhaven BI-DNDC manual describes negative refractive-index increments. Wyatt application note explains appropriate value depends solute, solvent, temperature wavelength. values synthetic declarations. absolute RI check runs injected-mass normalization, otherwise cancel constant gain error. two rows recover declared concentration positive negative dn_dc values. absolute value applied recorded signal.
code: time_min <- c(0, 1, 2, 4) concentration_g_ml <- c(0, 0.001, 0.002, 0) gain <- 2 input <- tibble::tibble(   sample_id = c("positive increment", "negative increment"),   dn_dc = c(0.2, -0.2) ) input$ri <- new_measure_list(lapply(input$dn_dc, function(increment) {   new_measure_tbl(time_min, concentration_g_ml * increment / gain) }))  ri_recipe <- recipe(~., data = input) |>   step_sec_ri(     measures = "ri", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc",     instrument_constant = gain, output_col = "concentration"   ) ri_result <- bake(prep(ri_recipe, training = input), new_data = NULL) stopifnot(   identical(ri_result$ri, input$ri),   identical(attr(ri_result$concentration, "sec_concentration_unit", exact = TRUE),             "g/mL") ) for (row in seq_len(nrow(input))) {   stopifnot(max(abs(ri_result$concentration[[row]]$value -                     concentration_g_ml)) < 1e-14) }

what: Declare the raw elution axis and concentration units
title: Qualify SEC detector units, delays and clipped signal
text: elution_units describes existing numeric location coordinates. accepts exactly "min", "s", "mL" "uL"; coordinates stay unchanged. Flow mL/min. concentration step multiplies sampled raw-axis area corresponding mL-per-axis-unit factor: table checks apply four declarations fixed 2 mg trace request output concentration units. location vectors constructed fixed minute values using declared coordinate scale; step rewrite . recovered mass recomputed baked curve requested units declared mL-per-axis-unit factor. exact coordinate checks confirm processing step left raw axis supplied. measure_record() stores axis declaration separately; pass knowledge explicitly elution_units building recipe.
code: axis_per_minute <- c(min = 1, s = 60, mL = 0.5, uL = 500) mL_per_axis_unit <- c(min = 0.5, s = 0.5 / 60, mL = 1, uL = 0.001) flow_ml_min <- 0.5 injected_mass_mg <- 2 output_units <- c("mg/mL", "g/mL")  mass_checks <- list() index <- 0L for (axis_unit in names(axis_per_minute)) {   raw_location <- time_min * axis_per_minute[[axis_unit]]   for (concentration_unit in output_units) {     measure_data <- data.frame(case_id = "known-2-mg")     measure_data$signal <- new_measure_list(list(       new_measure_tbl(raw_location, concentration_g_ml)     ))     mass_recipe <- recipe(~., data = measure_data) |>       step_sec_concentration(         measures = "signal",         injection_mass = injected_mass_mg,         flow_rate = flow_ml_min,         concentration_units = concentration_unit,         elution_units = axis_unit,         id = paste("guide_mass", axis_unit, gsub("/", "_", concentration_unit),                    sep = "_")       )     mass_result <- bake(       prep(mass_recipe, training = measure_data),       new_data = measure_data     )     curve <- mass_result$signal[[1]]     unit_tag <- attr(mass_result$signal, "sec_concentration_unit", exact = TRUE)     values_mg_ml <- curve$value     if (identical(concentration_unit, "g/mL")) {       values_mg_ml <- values_mg_ml * 1000     }     trapezoid_area <- sum(abs(diff(curve$location)) *       (head(values_mg_ml, -1) + tail(values_mg_ml, -1)) / 2)     recovered_mass_mg <- trapezoid_area * mL_per_axis_unit[[axis_unit]]     expected_values <- if (identical(concentration_unit, "mg/mL")) {       concentration_g_ml * 1000     } else {       concentration_g_ml     }     stopifnot(       identical(as.numeric(curve$location), raw_location),       identical(unit_tag, concentration_unit),       isTRUE(all.equal(curve$value, expected_values, tolerance = 1e-12,                        check.attributes = FALSE)),       abs(recovered_mass_mg - injected_mass_mg) < 1e-12     )     index <- index + 1L     mass_checks[[index]] <- data.frame(       elution_units = axis_unit,       concentration_unit = concentration_unit,       recovered_mass_mg = recovered_mass_mg     )   } } mass_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(mass_checks) knitr::kable(mass_table, digits = 8)

what: Check positive and negative delay direction
title: Qualify SEC detector units, delays and clipped signal
text: delay_times always expressed minutes delay_volumes mL, independent raw axis. recipe uses flow convert declarations axis. correction corrected(x) = target(x + delta) conversion raw axis. positive delay means target detector reads signal later, correction samples larger target coordinate. negative delay means target reads earlier samples smaller coordinate. Interpolation leaves coordinates fixed returns NA outside target’s supported range. new_measure_list(list(     new_measure_tbl(location, reference_values)   ))   result$target <- new_measure_list(list(     new_measure_tbl(location, target_values)   ))   attr(result$target, "sec_concentration_unit") <- tag   result }  delay_fit <- function(data, delay_value, declaration = "time",                       method = "interpolate", flow_rate = 0.5) {   delay_recipe <- arguments$delay_volumes <- c(target = delay_value)   }   do.call(step_sec_detector_delay, arguments) }  delay_location <- 0:5 reference_late <- c(0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0) target_late <- c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0) trace = "Target before correction",     location = delay_location,     value = target_early   ),   tibble::tibble(     case = "Target is 1 min early",     trace = "Target after correction",     location = negative_curve$location,     value = negative_curve$value   ) )  ggplot2::ggplot(   delay_plot,   ggplot2::aes(location, value, colour = trace, linetype = trace) ) + title: Getting Started with measure.sec
text: Size Exclusion Chromatography (SEC), also called Gel Permeation Chromatography (GPC), separates molecules hydrodynamic size. Larger molecules generally elute earlier smaller molecules. conventional calibration relates elution time volume molecular weight standards used. SEC chromatograms record detector response elution coordinate. measure.sec provides recipe steps processing RI, UV, light-scattering signals. scattering calculation single-angle; molecular weight estimate requires suitable concentration units detector calibration constant.

title: Getting Started with measure.sec
text: Recipes define sequence preprocessing steps. Think recipe blueprint analysis—describes , doesn’t yet. separation lets define workflow apply many samples.
code: # Start a recipe with your data # The formula specifies: predictor columns ~ grouping column # sample_id identifies which rows belong to each chromatogram rec <- recipe(   ri_signal + elution_time + dn_dc ~ sample_id,   data = ps_sample ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   # Convert the ri_signal column to measure format   # This step tells recipes how to interpret your chromatogram data   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   )

title: Getting Started with measure.sec
text: Chain additional steps using pipe (|>). step transforms data sequence:
code: rec <- recipe(   ri_signal + elution_time + dn_dc ~ sample_id,   data = ps_sample ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   # First: convert raw signal to measure format   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   ) |>   # Second: correct the baseline (removes drift and offset)   step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri") |>   # Third: process RI signal using the sample's dn/dc value   # Dividing by dn/dc converts the RI signal to concentration-proportional units   step_sec_ri(measures = "ri", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc")

title: Getting Started with measure.sec
text: Two functions execute recipe: prep(): Learns required parameters training data (like baseline fit coefficients) bake(): Applies transformations produce results source data synthetic assign units detector signal. plot uses elution-time support processing; panels separate vertical scales step_sec_ri() also scales response dn_dc. Synthetic PS-50K RI trace baseline correction dn/dc scaling. panels use measured elution-time locations; vertical scales independent, dataset specify signal units. prep() learns step parameters training data. bake() applies prepared recipe new data.
code: # Prep: Learn parameters from the data prepped <- prep(rec)  # Bake: Apply transformations (new_data = NULL means use the training data) result <- bake(prepped, new_data = NULL)  # View the processed data - ri contains the baseline-corrected, # dn/dc-scaled RI response result |>   select(sample_id, ri) #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #>   sample_id          ri #>   <chr>          <meas> #> 1 PS-50K    [2,001 × 2] raw_signal <- ps_sample |>   transmute(location = elution_time, value = ri_signal, stage = "Raw RI signal")  processed_signal <- result$ri[[1]] |>   transmute(location, value, stage = "Processed RI response")  stopifnot(identical(raw_signal$location, processed_signal$location))  bind_rows(raw_signal, processed_signal) |>   mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = c("Raw RI signal", "Processed RI response"))) |>   ggplot(aes(location, value)) +   geom_line(color = "#2E86AB", linewidth = 0.45) +   facet_wrap(vars(stage), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +   labs(     x = "Elution time (min)",     y = "Signal value (dataset scale)"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

title: Getting Started with measure.sec
text: common outputs SEC analysis molecular weight averages: - Mn (number-average): Emphasizes lower MW species - Mw (weight-average): Emphasizes higher MW species - Mz (z-average): Even sensitive high MW species - Dispersity (Mw/Mn): Measures breadth MW distribution (1.0 = monodisperse) Use step_sec_mw_averages() calculate . step_sec_conventional_cal(), pairs concentration trace calibrated MW curve; locations remain elution time volume. Alternatively, input trace can already use log₁₀(MW) axis. See Calibration section complete workflow.

title: Getting Started with measure.sec
text: SEC analysis requires calibration convert retention time molecular weight. common approach uses narrow standards—polymers known molecular weights low dispersity—build calibration curve. light-scattering workflow can estimate molecular weight without polymer standards suitable concentration units detector calibration constant. step_sec_mals() currently uses one angle; calculate Rg perform angular extrapolation. Calibration plot returned plot_sec_calibration() supplied synthetic polystyrene standards. cubic fit R-squared annotation summarize example standard set; retention shown across supplied range. Apply calibration using step_sec_conventional_cal(): example integrates portion within standards’ retention range. Signal outside range excluded, results may represent whole-sample averages. Conventional calibration assumes sample standard hydrodynamic behavior comparable; choose standards another calibration approach appropriate sample method.
code: # Load polystyrene narrow standards # These are well-characterized polymers used to build the calibration curve data(sec_ps_standards, package = "measure.sec")  # View the standards - each has a known peak molecular weight (Mp) sec_ps_standards |>   select(standard_name, mp, log_mp, retention_time) |>   print(n = 8) #> # A tibble: 16 × 4 #>   standard_name      mp log_mp retention_time #>   <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl>          <dbl> #> 1 PS-3150000    3150000   6.50           11.2 #> 2 PS-1870000    1870000   6.27           11.6 #> 3 PS-1090000    1090000   6.04           12.1 #> 4 PS-630000      630000   5.80           12.6 #> 5 PS-430000      430000   5.63           13.2 #> 6 PS-216000      216000   5.33           13.8 #> 7 PS-120000      120000   5.08           14.3 #> 8 PS-67500        67500   4.83           15.0 #> # ℹ 8 more rows  # Visualize the cubic calibration with the package plotting helper plot_sec_calibration(sec_ps_standards) +   labs(     x = "Retention time (min)",     y = expression(log[10](M[p] / Da)),     title = "Synthetic polystyrene standards"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) # Prepare standards in the format expected by the calibration step # Needs columns: retention (time/volume) and log_mw ps_cal <- sec_ps_standards |>   select(retention = retention_time, log_mw = log_mp)  rec_cal <- recipe(   ri_signal + elution_time + dn_dc ~ sample_id,   data = ps_sample ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   ) |>   step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri") |>   # Apply conventional calibration using polystyrene standards   # This creates a separate log10(MW) curve on the same elution axis   # fit_type options: "linear", "quadratic", "cubic" (most common)   step_sec_conventional_cal(     standards = ps_cal,     fit_type = "cubic"   ) |>   # Calculate MW averages from the calibrated chromatogram   # The averages step pairs the original signal with the calibrated curve   step_sec_mw_averages(integration_range = range(ps_cal$retention))  prepped_cal <- prep(rec_cal) #> Warning: Standard at 12.58 has 14.4% MW deviation. #> ℹ Consider removing outlier standards or using a different fit type. #> Warning: 1037 points (51.8%) are outside calibration range. #> ℹ Calibration range: 11.15 to 20.79 result_cal <- bake(prepped_cal, new_data = NULL)  # View molecular weight results # New columns are added with mw_ prefix result_cal |>   select(sample_id, mw_mn, mw_mw, mw_mz, mw_dispersity) #> # A tibble: 1 × 5 #>   sample_id mw_mn   mw_mw    mw_mz mw_dispersity #>   <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl> #> 1 PS-50K    1816. 205442. 1236629.          113.

Convert c to g/mL, then use the same equation as step_sec_lals/rals: #    MW = raw_signal * cal_constant / (K * c)  bsa_mw <- 66430  # g/mol (numerically equal to Da) bsa_conc_mg_ml <- 1.0 bsa_conc_g_ml <- bsa_conc_mg_ml / 1000 dn_dc_bsa <- 0.185 solvent_ri <- 1.333 wavelength <- 670  # Calculate K as in the current step implementation. Wavelength is converted # from nm to cm, and dn/dc is in mL/g (= cm^3/g). lambda_cm <- wavelength * 1e-7 K <- 4 * pi^2 * solvent_ri^2 * dn_dc_bsa^2 /   (6.022e23 * lambda_cm^4)  # For a measured raw_signal of 0.5, solve the API equation for the constant. raw_signal <- 0.5 calibration_constant <- bsa_mw * K * bsa_conc_g_ml / raw_signal

title: Size Exclusion Chromatography Analysis with measure.sec
text: Use step_sec_conventional_cal() fit calibration apply samples. step_sec_conventional_cal() Parameters: extrapolation = "none", stored MW curve finite sampled locations inside calibration domain. example selects finite sampled support one sample. nominal calibration endpoint falls samples, unsampled endpoint strip omitted; establish omitted mass negligible. Different sample grids need supported windows common range bracketed finite calibration values.
code: # Prepare standards for the step (needs 'retention' and 'log_mw' columns) ps_cal <- sec_ps_standards |>   select(retention = retention_time, log_mw = log_mp)  # Filter to a polystyrene sample for demonstration ps_sample <- sec_triple_detect |>   filter(sample_id == "PS-50K")  # Restrict this sample to measured locations inside the calibration domain. # A stored MW curve cannot supply off-grid endpoints beyond its finite samples. sampled_calibration_range <- range(ps_sample$elution_time[   ps_sample$elution_time >= min(ps_cal$retention) &     ps_sample$elution_time <= max(ps_cal$retention) ])  # Build the calibration recipe # Note: Use explicit formula with sample_id as the grouping variable rec_cal <- recipe(   ri_signal + elution_time + dn_dc ~ sample_id,   data = ps_sample ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   ) |>   step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri") |>   # Apply calibration to convert elution time to log(MW)   step_sec_conventional_cal(     measures = "ri",     standards = ps_cal,     fit_type = "cubic",     output_col = "mw",     extrapolation = "none"   ) |>   # Calculate MW averages from RI signal weighted by MW   step_sec_mw_averages(measures = "ri", integration_range = sampled_calibration_range)  # Prep and bake prepped <- prep(rec_cal) #> Warning: Standard at 12.58 has 14.4% MW deviation. #> ℹ Consider removing outlier standards or using a different fit type. result <- bake(prepped, new_data = NULL)  # View molecular weight results result |>   select(sample_id, mw_mn, mw_mw, mw_mz, mw_dispersity) #> # A tibble: 1 × 5 #>   sample_id mw_mn   mw_mw    mw_mz mw_dispersity #>   <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl> #> 1 PS-50K    1825. 205538. 1236629.          113.

text: tidy() method provides comprehensive diagnostics evaluating calibration quality: Review R², RMSE log molecular-weight scale, residual patterns, percent differences supplied values. universal cutoffs; use criteria defined method intended application.
code: # Get calibration diagnostics diagnostics <- tidy(prepped, number = 3)  # step_sec_conventional_cal is step 3  # Overview metrics diagnostics |>   select(fit_type, n_standards, r_squared, rmse_log_mw, max_abs_pct_deviation) #> # code: # Synthetic multi-detector workflow example # Note: MALS processing requires additional detector configuration rec_multi <- recipe(   ri_signal + uv_signal + mals_signal + elution_time + dn_dc + extinction_coef ~ sample_id,   # UV normalization requires a positive extinction coefficient.   data = dplyr::filter(sec_triple_detect, extinction_coef > 0) ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   # Convert each detector to measure format   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   ) |>   step_measure_input_long(     uv_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "uv"   ) |>   step_measure_input_long(     mals_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "mals"   ) |>   # No delay correction is applied; the package traces do not establish   # known input delays for an alignment example.   # Apply baseline correction   step_sec_baseline(measures = c("ri", "uv", "mals")) |>   # Process detectors   step_sec_ri(measures = "ri", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc") |>   step_sec_uv(measures = "uv", extinction_column = "extinction_coef") |>   # Convert to concentration before single-angle scattering   step_sec_concentration(     measures = "ri",     detector = "ri",     injection_volume = 100,       # µL     sample_concentration = 2.0,   # mg/mL     concentration_units = "mg/mL"   ) |>   # No scattering calibration supplied: output is relative and uncalibrated   step_sec_mals(mals_col = "mals", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc") #> Warning: No scattering calibration constant supplied; output is relative and #> uncalibrated.  prepped_multi <- prep(rec_multi) #> Warning: Negative detector values were excluded during mass normalization. #> ℹ 3335 of 20010 signal points (16.7%) were set to zero. #> ℹ Column "ri": maximum negative share of absolute sampled signal area was 3.4% #>   in row 1. result_multi <- bake(prepped_multi, new_data = NULL)  # View multi-detector results result_multi |>   select(sample_id, ri, uv, mals) |>   head(3) #> # A tibble: 3 × 4 #>   sample_id          ri          uv        mals #>   <chr>          <meas>      <meas>      <meas> #> 1 PS-1K     [2,001 × 2] [2,001 × 2] [2,001 × 2] #> 2 PS-10K    [2,001 × 2] [2,001 × 2] [2,001 × 2] #> 3 PS-50K    [2,001 × 2] [2,001 × 2] [2,001 × 2]

code: # Viscometer integration # This external input must include RI, differential-pressure (DP), and # inlet-pressure (IP) curves on a shared elution axis. Supply the settings # below from the method, sample record, and viscometer standard calibration. # dp_delay_ml, ip_delay_ml, flow_rate_ml_min, injection_volume_ul, # sample_concentration_mg_ml, viscometer_constant, left_baseline_fraction, # and right_baseline_fraction are method-specific. The baseline fractions must # cover peak-free regions for both RI and DP.  rec_visc <- recipe(~ ., data = visc_samples) |>   update_role(sample_id, dn_dc, new_role = "id") |>   # Convert the measured pressure and RI curves to measure columns   step_measure_input_long(ri_signal, location = vars(elution_time), col_name = "ri") |>   step_measure_input_long(dp_signal, location = vars(elution_time), col_name = "dp") |>   step_measure_input_long(ip_signal, location = vars(elution_time), col_name = "ip") |>   # Baseline-correct RI and DP in their recorded peak-free regions; retain IP   step_sec_baseline(     measures = c("ri", "dp"),     left_frac = left_baseline_fraction,     right_frac = right_baseline_fraction   ) |>   # Use target-minus-reference delays measured for these channels   step_sec_detector_delay(     reference = "ri",     targets = c("dp", "ip"),     delay_volumes = c(dp = dp_delay_ml, ip = ip_delay_ml),     flow_rate = flow_rate_ml_min,     elution_units = "min",     method = "interpolate"   ) |>   # Process the baseline-corrected RI response; IP keeps its positive reference   step_sec_ri(measures = "ri", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc") |>   # Use the calibrated viscometer constant and both pressure channels   step_sec_viscometer(     dp_col = "dp",     ip_col = "ip",     output_col = "specific_visc",     viscometer_constant = viscometer_constant   ) |>   # Concentration normalization updates the selected RI measure in place   step_sec_concentration(     measures = "ri",     detector = "ri",     injection_volume = injection_volume_ul,     sample_concentration = sample_concentration_mg_ml,     flow_rate = flow_rate_ml_min,     concentration_units = "mg/mL",     elution_units = "min"   ) |>   # The concentration column is still named ri after normalization   step_sec_intrinsic_visc(     specific_visc_col = "specific_visc",     concentration_col = "ri",     concentration_unit = "mg/mL",     units = "dL/g"   )  # After substituting method-specific inputs and standards: prepped_visc <- prep(rec_visc) result_visc <- bake(prepped_visc, new_data = NULL)

code: # Process each standard separately and find peak retention times process_standard <- function(std_data) {   std_name <- unique(std_data$standard_name)   mp <- unique(std_data$mp)    raw_peak_idx <- which.max(std_data$ri_mv)   raw_retention_time <- std_data$time_min[[raw_peak_idx]]   generator_retention_time <- 19 - 0.75 * log10(mp)    # Create recipe for baseline correction   rec <- recipe(ri_mv + time_min ~ standard_name, data = std_data) |>     update_role(standard_name, new_role = "id") |>     step_measure_input_long(       ri_mv,       location = vars(time_min),       col_name = "ri"     ) |>     step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri")    # Process   processed <- prep(rec) |> bake(new_data = NULL)    # Extract chromatogram data   chrom <- processed$ri[[1]]    # Find peak (maximum signal after baseline correction)   peak_idx <- which.max(chrom$value)   peak_time <- chrom$location[peak_idx]   peak_height <- chrom$value[peak_idx]    tibble(     standard_name = std_name,     mp = mp,     log_mp = log10(mp),     generator_retention_time = generator_retention_time,     raw_retention_time = raw_retention_time,     retention_time = peak_time,     peak_height = peak_height   ) }  # Process all standards peak_data <- sec_raw_standards |>   group_by(standard_name, mp) |>   group_split() |>   purrr::map(process_standard) |>   bind_rows() |>   arrange(desc(mp))  print(peak_data) #> # code: data(sec_triple_detect, package = "measure.sec") calibration_trace <- sec_triple_detect |>   filter(sample_id == "PS-50K")  calibration_recipe <- recipe(   ri_signal + elution_time ~ sample_id,   data = calibration_trace ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   step_measure_input_long(     ri_signal,     location = vars(elution_time),     col_name = "ri"   ) |>   step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri") |>   step_sec_conventional_cal(     measures = "ri",     standards = ps_cal,     fit_type = "cubic",     extrapolation = "none"   )  prepped_calibration <- prep(calibration_recipe) #> Warning: Calibration fit quality is low (R\u00b2 = 0.8324). #> ℹ Typical calibrations have R\u00b2 > 0.999. #> Warning: Standard at 15.67 has 484.9% MW deviation. #> ℹ Consider removing outlier standards or using a different fit type. # Use a temporary file here; replace it with a managed path in your workflow. cal_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") save_sec_calibration(   prepped_calibration,   file = cal_file,   metadata = list(     date = Sys.Date(),     column = "<column-id>",     instrument = "<instrument-id>",     mobile_phase = "<mobile-phase>",     flow_rate = "<flow-rate>",     temperature = "<temperature>"   ) ) #> ✔ Saved cubic calibration to /tmp/RtmpYnxfcu/file2b253acfcb89.rds

code: # Process delay standard with correction # Use the dataset's declared geometric delay volumes and minute coordinate axis. rec_aligned <- recipe(   ri_mv + uv_au + mals_mv + time_min + dn_dc ~ sample_id,   data = delay_std ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   # Convert each detector to measure format   step_measure_input_long(ri_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "ri") |>   step_measure_input_long(uv_au, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "uv") |>   step_measure_input_long(mals_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "mals") |>   # Apply baseline correction   step_sec_baseline(measures = c("ri", "uv", "mals")) |>   # Correct inter-detector delays   # A positive delay means the detector sees the sample after the reference.   step_sec_detector_delay(     reference = "ri",     targets = c("uv", "mals"),     delay_volumes = c(       uv = unique(delay_std$delay_uv_ml),       mals = unique(delay_std$delay_mals_ml)     ),     flow_rate = flow_rate,     elution_units = "min",     method = "interpolate"   )  aligned <- prep(rec_aligned) |> bake(new_data = NULL) # Extract and normalize aligned signals ri_chrom <- aligned$ri[[1]] uv_chrom <- aligned$uv[[1]] mals_chrom <- aligned$mals[[1]]  # Normalize each signal ri_norm <- ri_chrom$value / max(ri_chrom$value, na.rm = TRUE) uv_norm <- uv_chrom$value / max(abs(uv_chrom$value), na.rm = TRUE) mals_norm <- mals_chrom$value / max(mals_chrom$value, na.rm = TRUE)  # Build plot data aligned_plot <- tibble(   location = rep(ri_chrom$location, 3),   signal = c(ri_norm, uv_norm, mals_norm),   detector = rep(c("RI", "UV", "MALS"), each = length(ri_norm)) )  ggplot(aligned_plot, aes(location, signal, color = detector)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("RI" = "#2E86AB", "UV" = "#A23B72", "MALS" = "#F18F01")) +   labs(     x = "Time (min)",     y = "Normalized signal",     color = "Detector"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(legend.position = "bottom")

code: # Select a sample sample_1 <- sec_raw_multidetector |>   filter(sample_id == "Sample-1")  # Full triple detection recipe rec_triple <- recipe(   ri_mv + uv_au + mals_mv + time_min + dn_dc ~ sample_id,   data = sample_1 ) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   # Convert to measure format   step_measure_input_long(ri_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "ri") |>   step_measure_input_long(uv_au, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "uv") |>   step_measure_input_long(mals_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "mals") |>   # Baseline correction   step_sec_baseline(measures = c("ri", "uv", "mals")) |>   # Delay correction   step_sec_detector_delay(     reference = "ri",     targets = c("uv", "mals"),     delay_volumes = c(       uv = unique(delay_std$delay_uv_ml),       mals = unique(delay_std$delay_mals_ml)     ),     flow_rate = flow_rate,     elution_units = "min",     method = "interpolate"   ) |>   # Process RI for concentration   step_sec_ri(measures = "ri", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc")  result_sample <- prep(rec_triple) |> bake(new_data = NULL)  # View the processed data result_sample |>   select(sample_id, ri, uv, mals, dn_dc) #> # A tibble: 1 × 5 #>   sample_id           ri           uv         mals dn_dc #>   <chr>           <meas>       <meas>       <meas> <dbl> #> 1 Sample-1  [12,001 × 2] [12,001 × 2] [12,001 × 2] 0.185

title: Tutorial: Triple Detection from Raw Data
text: MALS estimate combines scattering response concentration optical inputs. basic relationship : Mw=RθK*⋅c⋅P(θ)M_w = \frac{R_\theta}{K^* \cdot c \cdot P(\theta)} : - RθR_\theta = excess Rayleigh ratio (MALS signal) - K*K^* = optical constant (depends dn/dc, wavelength) - cc = concentration (RI) - P(θ)P(\theta) = form factor (angular dependence) step_sec_mals() currently uses one angle assumes form factor approximately one. requires concentration curve known unit instrument calibration constant absolute estimates. Without calibration, output relative uncalibrated; step calculate Rg. MALS guide plots current API output documents limits.

title: Tutorial: Triple Detection from Raw Data
text: code records sample’s RI peak position supplied molecular-weight metadata. calculate compare molecular-weight estimate.
code: analyze_sample <- function(sample_data) {   sample_id <- unique(sample_data$sample_id)   known_mw <- unique(sample_data$mw)    rec <- recipe(     ri_mv + uv_au + mals_mv + time_min + dn_dc ~ sample_id,     data = sample_data   ) |>     update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>     step_measure_input_long(ri_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "ri") |>     step_measure_input_long(mals_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "mals") |>     step_sec_baseline(measures = c("ri", "mals")) |>     step_sec_detector_delay(       reference = "ri",       targets = "mals",       delay_volumes = c(mals = unique(sample_data$delay_mals_ml)),       flow_rate = flow_rate,       elution_units = "min",       method = "interpolate"     ) |>     step_sec_ri(measures = "ri", dn_dc_column = "dn_dc")    result <- prep(rec) |> bake(new_data = NULL)    # Extract peak info for summary   ri_chrom <- result$ri[[1]]   peak_idx <- which.max(ri_chrom$value)   peak_time <- ri_chrom$location[peak_idx]    tibble(     sample_id = sample_id,     known_mw = known_mw,     peak_time = peak_time,     dn_dc = unique(sample_data$dn_dc)   ) }  # Analyze all samples all_results <- sec_raw_multidetector |>   group_by(sample_id) |>   group_split() |>   purrr::map(analyze_sample) |>   bind_rows()  print(all_results) #> # A tibble: 4 × 4 #>   sample_id   known_mw peak_time dn_dc #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 PS-DelayStd   100000      15.6 0.185 #> 2 Sample-1       75000      14.6 0.185 #> 3 Sample-2      150000      14.1 0.085 #> 4 Sample-3       45000      16.0 0.15

title: Tutorial: Triple Detection from Raw Data
text: Baseline-corrected RI traces bundled raw example samples. Labels report dataset’s supplied molecular-weight metadata; curves molecular-weight calculations.
code: # Process all samples for plotting process_for_plot <- function(sample_data) {   sid <- unique(sample_data$sample_id)   known_mw <- unique(sample_data$mw)    rec <- recipe(     ri_mv + time_min + dn_dc ~ sample_id,     data = sample_data   ) |>     update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>     step_measure_input_long(ri_mv, location = vars(time_min), col_name = "ri") |>     step_sec_baseline(measures = "ri")    result <- prep(rec) |> bake(new_data = NULL)   chrom <- result$ri[[1]]    tibble(     location = chrom$location,     value = chrom$value,     sample_id = sid,     mw = known_mw,     label = paste0(sid, "\n(", scales::comma(known_mw), " Da)")   ) }  plot_data <- sec_raw_multidetector |>   group_by(sample_id) |>   group_split() |>   purrr::map(process_for_plot) |>   bind_rows()  ggplot(plot_data, aes(location, value, color = label)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +   labs(     x = "Elution time (min)",     y = "Baseline-corrected RI signal",     color = "Sample"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(legend.position = "right")

title: measure.sec
text: example creates three Gaussian signals known offsets linear baselines. UV 0.05 minutes earlier RI; scattering 0.15 minutes later. 1 mL/min, offsets also delay volumes mL. responses arbitrary simulated values. Give sample_id ID role keep one curve per sample detector. positive target delay moves signal earlier; negative delay moves later. Use measured delays flow rate acquisition. example shows correction convention; estimate instrument delay. Baseline subtraction uses recorded edge regions alignment. interpolated shift leaves NA target sampled. Known-offset simulated signals linear baseline subtraction detector-delay correction. correction, three peak maxima occur 10 minutes. Left right panels share response scale within detector; scales differ detectors. Concentration molecular-weight calculations need response calibration unit declarations. current step_sec_mals() calibrated single-angle approximation; multi-angle extrapolation radius gyration outside step’s implementation.
code: library(measure) library(measure.sec) library(recipes) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggplot2)  elution_time <- seq(9, 11, by = 0.01) gaussian <- function(centre) exp(-0.5 * ((elution_time - centre) / 0.12)^2) detector_data <- tibble(   sample_id = "illustrative-polymer",   elution_time,   ri_signal = 0.02 + 0.004 * (elution_time - 9) + gaussian(10),   uv_signal = 0.03 + 0.003 * (elution_time - 9) + 0.75 * gaussian(9.95),   mals_signal = 0.01 + 0.002 * (elution_time - 9) + 0.5 * gaussian(10.15) )  rec <- recipe(~ ., data = detector_data) |>   update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>   step_measure_input_long(ri_signal, location = vars(elution_time), col_name = "ri") |>   step_measure_input_long(uv_signal, location = vars(elution_time), col_name = "uv") |>   step_measure_input_long(mals_signal, location = vars(elution_time), col_name = "mals") |>   step_sec_baseline(measures = c("ri", "uv", "mals")) |>   step_sec_detector_delay(     reference = "ri",     delay_volumes = c(uv = -0.05, mals = 0.15),     flow_rate = 1,     elution_units = "min",     method = "interpolate"   )  prepped <- prep(rec) result <- bake(prepped, new_data = NULL) result |> select(sample_id, ri, uv, mals) #> # A tibble: 1 × 4 #>   sample_id                   ri        uv      mals #>   <chr>                   <meas>    <meas>    <meas> #> 1 illustrative-polymer [201 × 2] [201 × 2] [201 × 2] example_id <- "illustrative-polymer" raw_sample <- detector_data |> filter(sample_id == example_id) baked_sample <- result |> filter(sample_id == example_id)  raw_plot <- raw_sample |>   pivot_longer(ends_with("_signal"), names_to = "detector", values_to = "value") |>   transmute(     detector = sub("_signal$", "", detector),     location = elution_time, value, stage = "Recorded signals"   ) processed_plot <- bind_rows(lapply(c("ri", "uv", "mals"), function(detector) {   curve <- baked_sample[[detector]][[1]]   tibble(detector, location = curve$location, value = curve$value,          stage = "Aligned + baseline-corrected") })) plot_data <- bind_rows(raw_plot, processed_plot) |>   mutate(     detector = factor(detector, levels = c("ri", "uv", "mals"),                       labels = c("RI", "UV", "Scattering")),     stage = factor(stage, levels = c("Recorded signals", "Aligned + baseline-corrected"))   ) peak_time <- raw_sample$elution_time[which.max(raw_sample$ri_signal)]  ggplot(plot_data, aes(location, value, colour = stage)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.45, na.rm = TRUE) +   facet_grid(detector ~ stage, scales = "free_y") +   coord_cartesian(xlim = peak_time + c(-0.7, 0.7)) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +   labs(x = "Elution time (min)", y = "Simulated detector response") +   theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +   theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA))

title: Estimate Spreading Parameter from Narrow Standard — estimate_sigma
text: spreading parameter sigma represents standard deviation instrumental broadening function, assumed approximately Gaussian. best results, use narrow polydispersity standard (PDI < 1.05) run conditions samples. Method Details: gaussian: Fits Gaussian function peak using nonlinear least squares. accurate symmetric peaks. fwhm: Uses relationship sigma = FWHM / 2.355 Gaussian. Fast robust assumes symmetric peak. moments: Calculates sigma second central moment. Accounts asymmetry sensitive baseline.

text: g Numeric vector branching ratios g = Rg^2(branched) / Rg^2(linear). architecture Branching architecture model: "random": Random trifunctional branching (default) "star_3": 3-arm star polymer "star_4": 4-arm star polymer "star_f": f-arm star (requires arms parameter) "comb": Comb-like branching arms Number arms star polymers (required "star_f"). mw Optional molecular weight vector (length g) calculating total branches sample.

title: Calculate Branching Frequency from Zimm-Stockmayer Theory — measure_branching_frequency
text: data frame class branching_frequency containing: g Input branching ratio branches_per_molecule Estimated branch points per molecule branch_density Branches per unit MW (mw provided)

title: Calculate Branching Frequency from Zimm-Stockmayer Theory — measure_branching_frequency
text: Zimm-Stockmayer Theory: random trifunctional branching, relationship g average number branch points (n_b) : $$g = \left[\left(1 + \frac{n_b}{7}\right)^{1/2} + \frac{4n_b}{9\pi}\right]^{-1/2}$$ star polymers f arms: $$g = \frac{3f - 2}{f^2}$$ Interpretation: g = 1.0: Linear polymer (branching) g ~ 0.5-0.8: Lightly branched g ~ 0.3-0.5: Moderately branched g < 0.3: Highly branched/hyperbranched

title: Calculate Branching Frequency from Zimm-Stockmayer Theory — measure_branching_frequency
text: Zimm, B.H. Stockmayer, W.H. (1949). "Dimensions Chain Molecules Containing Branches Rings." J. Chem. Phys., 17, 1301-1314.

title: Calculate Branching Frequency from Zimm-Stockmayer Theory — measure_branching_frequency
code: # Calculate branching for random trifunctional polymer g_values <- c(0.9, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3) bf <- measure_branching_frequency(g_values) print(bf) #> Branching Frequency Analysis (Zimm-Stockmayer) #> ==================================================  #>  #> Architecture: random #> N samples: 4 #>  #> g ratio range: 0.300 - 0.900 #> Branches/molecule: 1.12 - 57.14 (mean: 19.74) #>  #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #>       g branches_per_molecule #>   <dbl>                 <dbl> #> 1   0.9                  1.12 #> 2   0.7                  5.12 #> 3   0.5                 15.6  #> 4   0.3                 57.1   # For star polymer with 4 arms bf_star <- measure_branching_frequency(0.625, architecture = "star_4")

code: measure_branching_index(   mw,   rg = NULL,   intrinsic_visc = NULL,   reference = "linear",   mh_linear = NULL,   rg_linear_fit = NULL,   method = c("g", "g_prime", "both") )

title: Calculate Branching Index — measure_branching_index
text: mw Numeric vector molecular weights branched samples. rg Numeric vector radius gyration values (g ratio). intrinsic_visc Numeric vector intrinsic viscosity values (g'). reference Type reference: either "linear" comparison linear polymer theory, data frame containing linear reference data. mh_linear Mark-Houwink parameters linear reference polymer (list K ). Required reference = "linear" using g'. rg_linear_fit Rg-MW relationship linear polymer: either model list slope intercept log(Rg) = intercept + slope * log(M). method Branching index type: "g": Radius gyration ratio: g = Rg^2(branched) / Rg^2(linear) "g_prime": Viscosity ratio: g' = [eta](branched) / [eta](linear) "": Calculate g g'

title: Calculate Branching Index — measure_branching_index
text: data frame columns: mw Molecular weight g Branching index Rg (calculated) g_prime Branching index viscosity (calculated) branches_per_molecule Estimated branch points (Zimm-Stockmayer)

title: Calculate Branching Index — measure_branching_index
text: Branching reduces hydrodynamic size polymers compared linear counterparts. quantified branching ratios: Rg-based branching index (g): $$g = \frac{R_g^2(branched)}{R_g^2(linear)}$$ Viscosity-based branching index (g'): $$g' = \frac{[\eta](branched)}{[\eta](linear)}$$ relationship g g' depends polymer architecture: $$g' = g^\epsilon$$ epsilon ~ 0.5-1.5 depending branching type. Zimm-Stockmayer Model (random branching): $$g = \frac{6}{n_b} \left[ \frac{1}{2} + \frac{(2 + n_b)^{1/2} - 1 - n_b/2}{n_b} \right]$$ n_b number branch points per molecule.

title: Calculate Branching Index — measure_branching_index
code: # Calculate branching index from Rg data mw <- c(100000, 200000, 500000) rg_branched <- c(12, 18, 32) rg_linear <- c(15, 22, 40)  # Reference linear polymer  g <- measure_branching_index(   mw = mw,   rg = rg_branched,   reference = data.frame(mw = mw, rg = rg_linear),   method = "g" )

title: Compare Branching Models — measure_branching_model_comparison
text: g Numeric vector experimental g ratios (Rg^2 branched / Rg^2 linear). mw Numeric vector molecular weights (length g). g_prime Optional numeric vector g' ratios (IV branched / IV linear). models Character vector models compare. Default compares : "random": Random trifunctional branching (Zimm-Stockmayer) "star": Star polymers (variable arms) "comb": Comb architecture "hyperbranched": Hyperbranched/dendritic branch_frequency fitting: assumed constant branching frequency (branches per 1000 Da). NULL, estimated data.

title: Compare Branching Models — measure_branching_model_comparison
text: list class branching_model_comparison containing: model_fits Data frame fit statistics model best_model Name best-fitting model predictions Data frame predicted g model experimental Input experimental data

title: Compare Branching Models — measure_branching_model_comparison
text: Model Equations: Random trifunctional (Zimm-Stockmayer): $$g = \left[\left(1 + \frac{n_b}{7}\right)^{1/2} + \frac{4n_b}{9\pi}\right]^{-1/2}$$ Star polymer (f arms): $$g = \frac{3f - 2}{f^2}$$ Comb polymer (n_b branches): $$g \approx \frac{1}{1 + 2n_b/3}$$ Hyperbranched (degree branching DB): $$g \approx \left(\frac{1}{1 + DB \cdot n/2}\right)^{0.5}$$ Model selection uses residual sum squares AIC-like criteria.

title: Compare Branching Models — measure_branching_model_comparison
text: Zimm, B.H. Stockmayer, W.H. (1949). J. Chem. Phys., 17, 1301-1314. Burchard, W. (1999). "Solution Properties Branched Macromolecules." Adv. Polym. Sci., 143, 113-194.

title: Compare Branching Models — measure_branching_model_comparison
code: # Compare models for branched polymer data mw <- c(50000, 100000, 200000, 500000) g_exp <- c(0.85, 0.72, 0.58, 0.42)  comparison <- measure_branching_model_comparison(g_exp, mw) print(comparison) #> Branching Model Comparison #> ============================================================  #>  #> Model Fit Summary: #> ------------------------------------------------------------  #>          model  parameter r_squared       rmse       aic #>         random 0.04648146 0.9887283 0.01699313 -17.24806 #>           star 1.11325520 0.9470407 0.03683411 -11.05914 #>           comb 0.00502421 0.9670907 0.02903611 -12.96221 #>  hyperbranched 0.09231394 0.9932768 0.01312403 -19.31498 #> ------------------------------------------------------------  #>  #> Best Model: hyperbranched (lowest AIC) #>   R-squared: 0.9933 #>   RMSE: 0.0131 #>   Parameter: 0.0923 #>  #> Note: Lower AIC indicates better fit with penalty for complexity. #> Consider physical plausibility when selecting the final model.

title: Estimate Mark-Houwink Parameters — measure_mh_parameters
text: Mark-Houwink equation relates intrinsic viscosity molecular weight: $$[\eta] = K \cdot M^$$ log form: $$\log([\eta]) = \log(K) + \cdot \log(M)$$ parameters K depend : Polymer-solvent system Temperature Polymer microstructure (tacticity, branching) Interpretation '' exponent: ~ 0.5: Theta solvent (polymer coil collapsed) ~ 0.5-0.8: Good solvent (typical range) ~ 0.8: Rigid rod extended chain < 0.5: Branched compact structures

title: Estimate Mark-Houwink Parameters — measure_mh_parameters
code: # Estimate Mark-Houwink parameters from triple-detection data mw <- c(10000, 25000, 50000, 100000, 250000) iv <- c(0.15, 0.28, 0.45, 0.72, 1.2)  mh <- measure_mh_parameters(mw, iv) print(mh) #> Mark-Houwink Parameters #> ========================================  #>  #> K = 3.8112e-04 #> a = 0.652 #>  #> R-squared: 0.9981 #> Data points: 5 #> MW range: 10000 - 250000 #>  #> Equation: [eta] = K * M^a # K = 0.000114, a = 0.716 (typical for PS in THF)

text: list class rg_mw_scaling containing: nu Scaling exponent (slope log-log space) prefactor Prefactor K Rg = K * M^nu r_squared R-squared fit conformation Interpreted polymer conformation n_points Number data points used fit lm fit object

title: Fit Rg-MW Scaling Relationship — measure_rg_mw_scaling
text: Rg-MW relationship follows power law: $$R_g = K \cdot M^{\nu}$$ nu (Flory exponent) indicates polymer conformation: Interpretation nu: nu ~ 0.33: Compact/spherical (collapsed globule) nu ~ 0.50: Theta solvent (ideal chain) nu ~ 0.588: Good solvent (swollen coil) nu ~ 1.0: Rigid rod Typical Values: Flexible polymers good solvent: nu = 0.55-0.60 Branched polymers: nu = 0.40-0.50 Proteins (globular): nu = 0.30-0.35 DNA: nu = 0.58-0.60

title: Fit Rg-MW Scaling Relationship — measure_rg_mw_scaling
text: Flory, P.J. (1953). "Principles Polymer Chemistry." Cornell University Press.

title: Fit Rg-MW Scaling Relationship — measure_rg_mw_scaling
code: # Fit Rg-MW for a linear polymer mw <- c(10000, 50000, 100000, 500000, 1000000) rg <- c(4.5, 12, 18, 45, 70)  # nm  scaling <- measure_rg_mw_scaling(mw, rg) print(scaling) #> Rg-MW Scaling Analysis #> ========================================  #>  #> Scaling Law: Rg = K * M^nu #>  #> nu (Flory exponent): 0.591 #>   95% CI: [0.574, 0.609] #> K (prefactor): 1.9661e-02 #>  #> Conformation: good solvent (swollen coil) #>  #> R-squared: 0.9997 #> Data points: 5 #> MW range: 10000 - 1000000

Default 30 cm. column_diameter Column inner diameter mm. Default 7.8 mm. flow_rate Flow rate mL/min (optional, linear velocity). particle_size Particle size micrometers (optional, reduced HETP). dead_volume Column dead volume mL (optional).

title: Column Performance Metrics for SEC — measure_sec_column_performance
text: list class sec_column_performance containing: separation_range MW range (exclusion limit total permeation) selectivity Slope log(MW) vs retention (mL^-1) hetp Height equivalent theoretical plate (mm) plates_per_meter Theoretical plates per meter reduced_hetp HETP/particle_size (particle_size provided) peak_capacity Estimated peak capacity separation range resolution_factor Resolution per decade MW

title: Column Performance Metrics for SEC — measure_sec_column_performance
text: Key SEC Column Performance Metrics: HETP (Height Equivalent Theoretical Plate): $$HETP = \frac{L}{N}$$ Reduced HETP (h): $$h = \frac{HETP}{d_p}$$ Optimal h ~ 2-3 well-packed columns. Selectivity (D): $$D = \frac{d \log M}{dV_R}$$ Higher D means better MW resolution. Peak Capacity: $$n_c = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{N}}{4} \ln\left(\frac{V_{exclusion}}{V_{total}}\right)$$ Typical Performance Guidelines: HETP: < 50 um analytical columns Reduced HETP: 2-5 good columns Plates/meter: > 20,000 HPLC SEC

title: Calculate Theoretical Plate Count — measure_sec_plate_count
text: retention Retention time peak. width Peak width. See width_type measurement method. width_type Type peak width measurement: "half_height" (default): Width 50% height (W0.5h) "baseline": Width baseline tangent lines (Wb) "inflection": Width inflection points (Wi) dead_time Column dead time (t0). provided, calculates effective plates (N_eff) using adjusted retention time.

title: Calculate Theoretical Plate Count — measure_sec_plate_count
text: Numeric plate count. Higher values indicate better efficiency.

title: Calculate Theoretical Plate Count — measure_sec_plate_count
text: Theoretical plate count measures column efficiency: Half-height width (common): $$N = 5.54 \left(\frac{t_R}{W_{0.5h}}\right)^2$$ Baseline width: $$N = 16 \left(\frac{t_R}{W_b}\right)^2$$ dead time correction (effective plates): $$N_{eff} = 5.54 \left(\frac{t_R - t_0}{W_{0.5h}}\right)^2$$ Typical SEC Performance: Analytical SEC columns: 10,000-40,000 plates/meter Preparative columns: 5,000-15,000 plates/meter UHPLC SEC: 50,000+ plates/meter

title: Calculate Peak Resolution — measure_sec_resolution
text: Calculates resolution two chromatographic peaks using USP EP formula.

title: Calculate Peak Resolution — measure_sec_resolution
code: measure_sec_resolution(   retention_1,   retention_2,   width_1,   width_2,   width_type = c("baseline", "half_height", "tangent"),   method = c("usp", "ep") )

title: Calculate Peak Resolution — measure_sec_resolution
text: retention_1 Retention time first peak (earlier eluting). retention_2 Retention time second peak (later eluting). width_1 Peak width first peak. See width_type units. width_2 Peak width second peak. width_type Type peak width measurement: "baseline" (default): Width baseline (Wb) "half_height": Width half height (W0.5h) "tangent": Width tangent lines inflection points method Resolution formula use: "usp" (default): Rs = 2(t2 - t1) / (w1 + w2) "ep": Rs = 1.18(t2 - t1) / (w1_0.5h + w2_0.5h)

title: Calculate Peak Resolution — measure_sec_resolution
text: Numeric resolution value. Rs > 1.5 indicates baseline separation.

title: Calculate Peak Resolution — measure_sec_resolution
text: Resolution quantifies degree separation adjacent peaks: USP Formula (baseline width): $$R_s = \frac{2(t_2 - t_1)}{W_{b1} + W_{b2}}$$ EP Formula (half-height width): $$R_s = \frac{1.18(t_2 - t_1)}{W_{0.5h,1} + W_{0.5h,2}}$$ Interpretation: Rs < 1.0: Peaks overlap significantly Rs = 1.0: ~94% separation (4 sigma) Rs = 1.5: Baseline separation (~99.7%) Rs > 2.0: Complete separation gap

title: Calculate Peak Resolution — measure_sec_resolution
code: # Calculate resolution between monomer and dimer measure_sec_resolution(   retention_1 = 8.2,   # dimer (elutes first in SEC)   retention_2 = 9.5,   # monomer   width_1 = 0.4,   width_2 = 0.5 ) #> [1] 2.888889

title: Universal Calibration for SEC — step_sec_universal_cal
text: Universal calibration based principle polymers hydrodynamic volume elute retention time, regardless chemical structure. hydrodynamic volume proportional [eta]M: $$V_h \propto [\eta] \cdot M$$ Universal Calibration Curve: $$\log([\eta] \cdot M)_{sample} = \log([\eta] \cdot M)_{standard}$$ retention volume, using Mark-Houwink equations: $$[\eta] = K \cdot M^$$ can solve sample MW: $$M_{sample} = \left(\frac{K_{std} \cdot M_{std}^{1+a_{std}}}{K_{sample}}\right)^{\frac{1}{1+a_{sample}}}$$ Mark-Houwink Parameters (THF, 25C): Polystyrene: K = 0.000114, = 0.716 PMMA: K = 0.000128, = 0.690 Polyisoprene: K = 0.000251, = 0.728 Polybutadiene: K = 0.000457, = 0.693
